text: Received orders for lifeguard the next day.
Posit Lat. 24-05N, Long. 122-06E.
Surfaced on lifeguard station. Sky completely overcast with strong wind and rough seas.

Sighted B-24 at about 8 miles on westerly course. He gave no indication of having seen us. No other planes were sighted, and nothing heard on VHF. It seems probable that scheduled strikes were called off on account of weather.
Sighted and exchanged calls with patrolling B-24. He had nothing to report.
Surfaced. Barometer high, but seas still state 5 to 6 from NNE with heavy overcast.
Sighted PB4Y heading southeast.
Posit Lat. 24-34N, Long. 122-47E.
Surfaced. Weather clear and seas moderating.
Received orders to leave present lifeguard station and proceed to point in vicinity of Sakishima Gunto to search for downed aviators. Proceeding at four engine speed.

Southwest of Iriomote Jima encountered strong 156 mc radar interference similar to that encountered by BATFISH on Jap submarine (see section U). Swung ship to determine bearing, but found it to be emanating from the island.

(Section U intercept log, ship position 24°06'N 125°14'E as typed: 156 mc, PRF 500, pulse width 10, antenna rotation irregular; second entry same time and position:) This had the looks of a 103MC carrier modulated with 100% modulation at 350 CPS. It made constant sweeps at 1 R.P.M. Maybe a Jap radar beacon - land based. (As typed, 24-06N 125-14E is about 40 nm south of Miyako Jima, not southwest of Iriomote Jima as the narrative says at 2150. It does fit the run from the 21 Apr noon position at four-engine speed (about 135 nm east in 7.6 h); unresolved.)
Arrived at reported position of downed aviators and commenced search southeast of Ishigaki Jima.
Began feeling distant explosions and seeing occasional flashes, presumed to be carrier planes striking Ishigaki Jima and Miyako Jima.

Began making contact with carrier planes. Requested information on any downed aviators and after a brief flurry of communications learned that we were within 20 miles of a downed Hellcat pilot in rubber boat. Planes furnished cover and guided us in.

Took aboard Ensign Donald E. Corzine, file #382983, U.S.S. CHENANGO Hellcat pilot. He had been in the water fourteen hours but was in excellent condition and very glad to be aboard. Replacement clothing was no problem except for his size thirteen shoes. ... this rescue did more for the morale of the crew than anything else could have done with the exception of sinking ships. Every officer and man is proud to have been of some help to those who are now the ball carriers. (No position or cause of loss given. Fourteen hours before 0737 I puts him in the water about 1737 I on 21 Apr.)
Proceeding with search for downed aviators previously reported in our orders.
Released fighter cover. Thereafter during the day numerous planes were contacted, mostly flying high enroute to or from their carriers.
Posit Lat. 24-03N, Long. 124-16E.
(Section U intercept log, ship position 24°01'N 124°12'E: 104 mc, PRF 350, pulse width very wide, antenna rotation 1.) The full scale sweep is as seen in the sketch. Made regular sweeps.

Completed search of probable southern sector. Dove and headed north, intending to transit the channel to eastward of Ishigaki Jima immediately after dark and continue search to northward. Strong northerly winds yesterday would have driven survivors to southwest, but with moderation of weather the northerly current would have taken charge.
Surfaced.

Received orders to return to our assigned lifeguard station to the northeast of Formosa. Proceeding westward. Learned later that the survivors for whom we had been searching had been picked up by a PBM.
Submerged on station.
Sighted unidentified single engine fighter plane on westerly course.
Posit Lat. 24-40N, Long. 122-37E.
(Section U intercept log, ship position 24°20'N 122°32'E:) Same intercepts as 2230, 13 April. 0400, 18 April.
Dove for SJ contact at 4000 yds, moving in fast, nothing in sight. Suspected a plane, although APR had indicated no radars other than the customary assorted land-based air search equipment.
(Section U intercept log, ship position 24°38'N 122°27'E: 155 mc, came on suddenly.) A plane contact was made on the SJ shortly after this intercept was made.

Surfaced; all clear. During remainder of night we made numerous other close-in contacts, moving at various speeds. A check for phantoms ... showed they were real pips. ... My only explanation is that they possibly were porpoises or blackfish, of which a large number were seen during the daytime.
